newsitem.title: USA: CSCE cocoa called to open little changed.
newsitem.headline: CSCE cocoa called to open little changed.

text.p: CSCE cocoa futures were called to open little changed Thursday after an uneventful performance in London, traders said.

LIFFE cocoa futures were mostly weaker early Thursday in rangebound dealings, with September down three stg at the midday break at 1,115 stg a tonne after posting trades from 1,115 to 1,111 stg. Spot July rose two stg to 1,100 stg.
Wednesday, New York cocoa futures ended sharply lower, pressured by trade selling and profit taking amid improving weather in top-grower Ivory Coast.
CSCE September settled down $24 at $1,601 a tonne after ranging from $1,623 and $1,599. Spot July fell $33 to $1,551, while the back months finished down $22 to $24.

Technically, near-term support for September was pegged at $1,598-$1,595. A stronger downside hurdle was seen at $1,577, with a chart gap looming between $1,540 and $1,516. On the upside, resistance was put at $1,625-$1,629, they said.

On the fundamental front, Ivorian cocoa industry and crop analysts will wait until August to see if El Nino weather pattern emerges in West Africa. Most analysts downplayed the possible effects, expecting any dry weather to emerge after the 1997/98 main crop (Oct-April) setting.

Preliminary 1997/98 crop estimates range from what traders said was a bearish 786,000 tonnes (main crop) by U.S.-based crop analyst Hans Kilian to 1.1 million tonnes for the entire 1997/98 harvest by Swiss chocolate giant Callebaut Barry, which has two factories in Ivory Coast.
Ivory Coast, the world's largest cocoa grower, produced a bumper 1.2 million tonnes in 1995/96.

Meanwhile, Ivorian cocoa arrivals into ports have slowed to a rate of 5,000-7,000 tonnes a week since mid-May but July is expected to propel volumes towards a mid-crop (May-Sept) forecast range of 150,000-180,000 tonnes, industry sources said on Thursday.
